source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2024) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study (arXiv 2305.03731)
finding: gpt-3.5-turbo shows a human-like drop on verbal and spatial n-back as n goes 1 to 3. Sensitivity d' falls to about 1 at n=3, the same place human performance drops.
numbers: temperature 1; 50 blocks per n in {1,2,3} per condition; d' about 1 at n=3 in three of four verbal variants (base, and the other non-noise variants).
limits: Only gpt-3.5 tested in depth; task comprehension not controlled (see c03). Later work shows weaker models may be doing a different k-back task.
agent_relevance: A hard n=3 style limit on tracking exact lagged items is plausible for the agent too; do not rely on the model to hold more than a few items in mind without writing them down.

source: Gong et al. (2024) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: noise and grid-size variants
finding: Adding 3-6 random noise characters to each trial lowered capacity significantly, like distractors in human studies. Larger spatial grids gave higher d' (less interference between items).
numbers: noise variant is the only verbal variant that does not reach capacity near 3; bigger grid gave higher d' (Fig. 8).
quote: The LLM has a higher working memory capacity when the grid size is larger
limits: Authors say the grid-size effect needs a human control; no effect sizes reported in text.
agent_relevance: Distractor text in the working context hurts retrieval. Keep the active slot small and clean; strip noise before it enters the prompt.

source: Gong et al. (2024) model comparison across 8 LLMs
finding: GPT-4 had far higher n-back capacity than gpt-3.5. Open 6-13B models (Bloomz, ChatGLM, Vicuna) had very low capacity and were nearly indistinguishable. The authors argue n-back score correlates with general model ability.
numbers: GPT-4 tested only up to n=3 because of cost, so its exact limit is unknown.
limits: Open models may have failed on task understanding, not memory (see c04).
agent_relevance: N-back style probes can serve as a cheap capability gate when picking which model fills a slot.

source: Hu and Lewis (2025) Do Language Models Understand the Cognitive Tasks Given to Them? N-Back Paradigm (arXiv 2412.18120)
finding: Poor n-back scores in weaker models are partly a task-comprehension and task-set-maintenance failure. Their errors fit a different m-back rule (m not equal n). Three tiers appear: T3 below 20% on 2- and 3-back, T2 about 50% (2-back) and 40% (3-back), T1 above 80%.
numbers: Llama 3.1 70B Instruct (T1), Gemma 2 27B (T2), Qwen 1.5 14B (T3). Zero-shot with instructions only, T1 still inferred the task. Qwen 1.5 14B could not get two consecutive correct answers after 10 demo sequences in interactive training.
quote: poor performance is due at least in part to a limitation in task comprehension and task set maintenance
limits: Challenges Gong et al. directly. Open models only.
agent_relevance: A failure on a slot may be a task-set failure, not a capacity limit. Give worked examples and check the model did the asked task before reading the result as a memory limit.

source: Hu and Lewis (2025) harder n and prompting strategies
finding: Llama 3.1 70B degrades gradually, not at a cliff. Prepending a ladder of demonstrations (1-back up to n-back) lifts large-n results. An interactive demo with feedback helps middle models.
numbers: exact-retrieval accuracy 75.25% at n=8 (no ladder); with ladder: retrieval 79.83%, 80.17%, 71.67% and task accuracy 90.08%, 90.08%, 84.75% for n=8, 9, 10.
limits: One strong model; no human control at n=8-10. Attention in Llama models was diffuse (max mean retrieval attention under 10%) versus Qwen 2 72B at 71.98%.
agent_relevance: Staged demonstrations of the lag task raise effective capacity a lot at zero training cost; an example-ladder is a cheap scaffold for any lag-based tracking.

source: Gong and Zhang (2024) Self-Attention Limits Working Memory Capacity of Transformer-Based Models (arXiv 2409.10715)
finding: Small decoder-only transformers trained from scratch on N-back lose accuracy as N rises. Attention entropy rises with N, so attention gets more dispersed. A 1-layer 1-head model shows a significant decline; bigger models stay above 95% but still slip slightly.
numbers: 1-layer 1-head: Kruskal-Wallis H=38.517, p<.001, eta-squared=0.248; extended to N=6 shows a logarithmic decline.
limits: Toy models trained on one task; later work (c07, c08) shows the limit in LLMs is in readout, not in locating the target.
agent_relevance: Weak support for a mechanistic cap on lagged lookup; treat as a hypothesis, not a design rule.

source: Gong (2026) Language Models Share a Readout Bottleneck in Working Memory (arXiv 2610.21176)
finding: Across 15 LLMs (70M to 14B) n-back sensitivity falls with N and errors concentrate on lures. The target-tracking attention heads usually find the right item; the limit is reading it out under interference.
numbers: median d' 2.57 at N=1, 0.91 at N=4, 0.52 at N=6; Qwen2.5-14B 4.28 at N=1 but 1.15 at N=6. At N=2 models say match to a median 79% of N-1 lures versus 4% of other non-matches. Heads attend off target on only 16%, 7%, 8% of misses at N=2,3,4.
limits: Models up to 14B only; preprint; one task. Chat-format check (Qwen2.5-Instruct 0.5-7B) gave same decline (d' 1.8-2.0 at N=1, 0.4-0.7 at N=6).
agent_relevance: The limit is interference, not lookup. Remove competing look-alike items from the active slot rather than telling the model to look harder.

source: Gong (2026) readout bottleneck: interventions
finding: Sharpening attention gives negligible gains. Suppressing the letter identity of non-target items raises d' in nearly all model-by-load cells. Linear probes decode whether a match was at target or lure even on trials where the model false-alarms.
numbers: distractor suppression median +0.44 d' at N=4 (43 cells), false alarms fall from about 0.2-0.3 to about 0.1 with hit rate barely changed; random subspace -0.03; removing the target letter -1.54; the earlier single-direction removal of Xiong et al. gave +0.11 (about a fifth). Wilcoxon p<1e-8.
limits: Needs access to hidden states and to know the target, so it is a causal test, not a deployable method.
agent_relevance: Information is present but not used. Supports G3/G4 style outside checks: code can compare positions exactly where the model confuses neighbours.

source: Xiong et al. (2026) In-context superposition: human-like working memory interference in LLMs (arXiv 2604.09670, COLM 2026)
finding: A 2-layer transformer trained on N-back solves it perfectly, yet diverse pretrained LLMs decline with load, show recency bias, and are hurt by lure and set-size effects. Better N-back accuracy goes with better benchmark scores.
numbers: Pearson r of mean N-back accuracy (N=1-4, 10 models) with MMLU Pro .78/.70, GPQA Diamond .88/.72, IFEval .69/.82 (autoregressive/teacher forced). Interference manipulations vs accuracy: lure r=-.51/-.32, stimulus set size r=-.30/-.26. Lure probability 0.25 (items from t-(N-1) or t-(N+1)).
limits: n=10 models so wide intervals; correlation not cause. Suppression gains were larger in weaker models, selected and tested on same trials.
agent_relevance: Confirms the human parallel: capacity equals selection under interference, and tracks general ability. Good argument for small, clean working slots.

source: Liang, Zhu, Wang, Zhou (2026) Can Vision Replace Text in Working Memory? Spatial n-Back in VLMs (arXiv 2602.04355)
finding: On spatial n-back with Qwen2.5 and Qwen2.5-VL, text-grid input beats image-grid input in accuracy and d'. Nominal 2- and 3-back often act like 1-back (recency-locked comparison): evidence AUC peaks at lag 1 rather than the instructed lag.
numbers: ordering LLM(text) > VLM(text) > VLM(vision) held in Qwen2.5-32B and Llama 3.1-8B/3.2-11B-Vision pairs; AUC at instructed lag falls to about 50% at n=2,3. In 3x3 grids over half of blocks gave 0% match responses.
limits: Qwen and Llama pairs only; sensitivity depends on grid size (denser repeats hurt).
agent_relevance: Storing state as images (visual memory tricks) costs accuracy for exact updates. Keep exact working state as text.

source: Liang et al. (2026) grid size and recent repeats
finding: Larger grids improve 1-back sensitivity because lures become rarer. In small grids recent-repeat density lowers match evidence and can trigger an always-non-match policy.
numbers: lure-match trials show a low-evidence mode in small grids; 3x3 collapse in over half of blocks (median match response rate 0%).
limits: Single paradigm; interprets log-probability evidence, not human data.
agent_relevance: Accuracy alone hides recency-locked shortcuts; our harness should score by lure type, not only total accuracy.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference in LLMs (PI-LLM, arXiv 2506.08184)
finding: Stream key-value updates and ask for the last value of each key. Retrieval accuracy falls log-linearly toward zero as old values pile up, even though the answer is just before the query. Errors are stale overwritten values.
numbers: models 0.6B to 637B; update counts 3 to 400; 46 keys tracked; llama4-maverick near 100% at few keys but about 5% when tracking 46 keys; value length near 40 words drops accuracy under 5%.
limits: Synthetic key-value streams; reasoning models excluded from the regression for latency (over 200 s per task).
agent_relevance: A scratchpad full of superseded values will return old values. Overwrite in place or delete old entries in code; do not append updates and hope the model picks the latest.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) PI-LLM: size versus context length, prompts
finding: Interference Endurance Score rises with parameter count but not with nominal context window. MoE models match or underperform dense models of the same total size. Prompts telling the model to forget or ignore earlier input give limited help and make errors cluster near the forget point.
numbers: regression of IES on parameters and context length: size significant, context length not; forget/ignore prompts ('forget' condition, Fig. 11) did not raise accuracy.
limits: Prompt variants tested are few; no human directed-forgetting numbers given here.
agent_relevance: Telling the model to forget does not work (matches G2 and G6 spirit: use code). Remove stale items from the prompt itself.

source: Huang, Sun, Wang, Dredze (2025) Language Models Do Not Have Human-Like Working Memory (arXiv 2505.10571)
finding: Across 17 frontier models, tasks that need a number kept private (number guessing, yes/no deduction, math magic) show contradictory behavior. Models almost never say Yes to a guess and prefer seven when they do. They answer as if estimating the chance a human guess is right.
numbers: 17 models in four families; 'Yes' almost never produced in the number-guessing game; math magic: step-by-step CoT lifts base models to 10-30% accuracy, DeepSeek-R1 100%; 66.7% of o1-Mini correct answers, 46.9% of o3-Mini and 68.5% of o4-Mini involve the number seven.
limits: Behavioural inference about latent state; authors argue n-back lets models use the visible context, so it is not a clean test.
agent_relevance: Anything the agent must keep hidden or implicit should be written outside the model (in code state). Do not rely on private latent state across turns.

source: Zhang, Jian, Ouyang, Vosoughi (2024) Working Memory Identifies Reasoning Limits in Language Models (EMNLP 2024, main.938)
finding: Scales InstructGPT/GPT-3.5/GPT-4 on n-back and Big-Bench Hard. Small models collapse (copy input format, or output one symbol repeatedly), and a U-shaped scaling appears. Code training (text-davinci-002) raised n-back scores over davinci-001. Humans keep d' of 3.39-4.05 on 4x4 grids.
numbers: human d' 3.39 to 4.05 in 4x4 grid at n=1,2,3; 23 BBH tasks; error-analysis-based CoT+ prompts beat answer-only, CoT, AutoCoT, PS, ToT in their Fig. 1. Exact BBH accuracy numbers not read in text extract.
limits: Hu and Lewis argue its n-back sets all stimuli at once, not a standard paradigm; CoT+ was hand-built from error analysis.
agent_relevance: For small models use short answer-only prompts; complex scaffolds can hurt them. Hand-fixed step patterns (chunking, step reminders) help bigger models.

source: Dsouza, Glaze, Shin, Sala (2024) Evaluating Language Model Context Windows: A Working Memory Test (SWiM, arXiv 2407.03651)
finding: On eight long-context models, GPT-4 and Claude 3 Opus lose accuracy when the answer document sits in the middle (lost in the middle). Medoid voting (shuffle documents several times, take the answer closest to the others) recovers part of the loss.
numbers: up to 24% accuracy lift on single-document QA; distractor share varied 0, 25, 50, 75, 100% of the context.
limits: Synthetic Cosmopedia documents with GPT-4 written QA; medoid voting costs k calls. Same-model samples are not independent (G4).
agent_relevance: Position in the active context matters; put the item the next step needs at the edges, and place key facts last.

source: Wang et al. (2026, Mar) WMIP: Working-Memory-Inspired Probe of Cumulative State Tracking (arXiv 2603.27343)
finding: 18 LLMs asked to track a state through 3 to 100 updates without writing steps. Core accuracy is far below single-step arithmetic and falls with length. From 50 updates no model exceeds 10%. Asking for written steps raises accuracy a lot.
numbers: core items 31.7% vs single-step arithmetic 84.9%; K=3 44.4% down to K=100 0.8%; written steps and last-line answer reach 88.0% (950/1,080 on 60 shared items), most of the gain from the instruction rather than the larger budget (budget added 195 correct, instructions 400 more); Kendall tau-b with BFCL 0.417-0.449.
limits: Correlation with BFCL does not single out state tracking (core minus arithmetic differences include zero).
agent_relevance: The strongest single scaffold finding: write the running state after each update. Our program should hold the state and the model should do one update per call.

source: WMIP: query types and sets/counts
finding: Assignment-style state (colour, location, status) is tracked well but sets and counts are hard. Output protocol changes measured accuracy.
numbers: assignment accuracy 90.0% vs 54.1% for sets and counts; meeting counts 34.1%, inventory 64.6%.
limits: Parser 1 numbers; parsers differ slightly.
agent_relevance: Counting and set membership should be done in code (matches section 1 of the schema: the program counts).

source: Wang et al. (2024) Symbolic Working Memory Enhances Language Models for Complex Rule Application (arXiv 2408.13654)
finding: A neurosymbolic loop stores facts and rules in natural language and in symbols in an external memory. Code grounds applicable rules each step and the LLM applies them. It beats scratchpad CoT, SC-CoT, Self-Notes, Logic-LM and SymbCoT on multi-step rule application.
numbers: (pdftotext table order assumed GPT-4/GPT-3.5 per dataset) CLUTRR 92.34% vs scratchpad CoT 83.83% (GPT-4), 78.72% vs 57.02% (GPT-3.5); ProofWriter 77.33% vs 61.33% (GPT-4), 58.00% vs 49.67% (GPT-3.5); AR-LSAT 70.00% vs 41.25% (GPT-4); Boxes tracking 100% shown in the table.
limits: Column assignment read from a flattened table; GPT-3.5 AR-LSAT cell not verified. Logic-LM re-implemented on a harder subset.
agent_relevance: Direct match to our design: an external store plus code-made grounding step beats pure chain of thought on multi-step rule use.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Improving Factuality with Explicit Working Memory (Ewe, arXiv 2412.18069)
finding: A working memory of KV-cache units holds retrieved passages and fact-checking feedback, refreshed during generation. It raises factuality over RAG, FLARE-style and CoVe baselines without lowering helpfulness.
numbers: VeriScore +2 to +6 points absolute on four long-form datasets (Llama-3.1 70B base); effect smaller on 8B; human check, Cohen kappa above 0.61 for VeriScore vs human labels; memory-unit count, unit length and retrieval threshold all matter.
limits: Needs model-internal memory units and a fact-check pipeline; gains modest.
agent_relevance: Refreshing the active memory from outside checks mid-generation is an agent-loop version of a central executive that updates a limited buffer.

source: Authors not checked (2023) Empowering Working Memory for Large Language Model Agents (arXiv 2312.17259)
finding: A conceptual blueprint mapping Baddeley's multicomponent model (central executive, sketchpad, loop, episodic buffer) onto an LLM agent with a central working-memory hub and episodic buffer for cross-episode memory. No experiments.
numbers: none; position paper
limits: No measurement; the LLM is the central processor, which our schema forbids as decision-maker.
agent_relevance: Shows the mapping people propose. Our version keeps the executive in code, not in the model. Do not borrow the hub as an unmeasured box.

source: Hu and Lewis (2025) / Gong (2026) contrast on the cause of the n-back decline
finding: Three competing explanations for the LLM n-back decline: a capacity limit from dispersed attention (Gong & Zhang), a task-comprehension failure (Hu & Lewis), and interference at readout (Gong 2026, Xiong 2026). Evidence in 2026 favours interference for strong models and comprehension for weak ones.
numbers: k-back rule that best fits answers differs from instructed N in only 14 of 90 cases, all at N>=4 in small models (Gong 2026); Hu & Lewis tiers T1-T3 above.
limits: Explanations are not exclusive; different model sizes tested.
agent_relevance: Test the model on the task rule first (cheap check), then interference.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) CoT+ and small-model findings
finding: Small LMs do better with simple answer-only prompts than with AutoCoT, PS or ToT. Larger models gain from error-derived prompts that add chunking and step reminders. The gap to human performance remains.
numbers: 23 Big-Bench Hard tasks; small models text-ada/babbage/curie often drop with advanced prompts. Exact accuracies not extracted.
limits: EMNLP version; numbers in figures only.
agent_relevance: The scaffold must be matched to the model size; heavy scaffolds are not free (G7).

source: Gong et al. (2024) instruction strategies keep the capacity limit
finding: Different instruction strategies were tried and the basic n-back capacity pattern persisted; the abstract states the fundamental pattern of a capacity limit persists across them.
numbers: abstract-level statement; per-strategy numbers not extracted.
limits: Only prompt-level changes; conflicts with Hu & Lewis, where demonstrations and an example ladder changed results a lot (c05).
agent_relevance: Prompt wording alone is a weak lever; structure (examples, external state) is the stronger one.

source: Xiong et al. (2026) suppression intervention
finding: Removing letter-identity directions of competing items improves N-back in five LLMs; gains are larger in weaker models.
numbers: aggregate gains in both autoregressive and teacher-forced evaluation; configuration chosen and evaluated on same trials; later replication (Gong 2026) found about a fifth of the gain (+0.11 d') when configuration was chosen on calibration sequences.
limits: Possible overfitting of the search; not a prompt method.
agent_relevance: Supports clearing look-alike items; the effect is smaller than first reported.

source: Dsouza et al. (2024) SWiM: effect of distractors
finding: Adding distractor documents (0 to 100% of context) lowers single-document QA accuracy; position of the answer matters too.
numbers: distractor levels 0, 25, 50, 70/75, 100%; per-model curves in figures only.
limits: Numbers not extracted from text.
agent_relevance: Fewer, cleaner items in the prompt beat more items; supports an active-slot budget.
